profiles.meeting_scenario: CloudCore, a B2B infrastructure platform, is planning an MVP for a new customer onboarding portal that will replace the current mix of email threads, spreadsheets, and support tickets used to provision enterprise accounts. The meeting is a planning session between product and engineering after a stakeholder workshop produced a 'requirements' list for the pilot. The agenda is to decide what will be included in the MVP, how the team will document the agreed requirements, who owns each workstream, and what 'pilot-ready' means for a deployment targeted for the end of the next sprint. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for the MVP scope, documentation, implementation approach, and timeline for launching with two design-partner customers.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Enterprise SaaS product discovery, customer onboarding workflows, stakeholder alignment
members.background: Nina previously worked in customer success operations and moved into product management two years ago; she is leading the onboarding portal because she knows the pain points of the current manual provisioning process and has been collecting requests from sales, support, and compliance.
members.private_state: Nina wants to preserve momentum from the stakeholder workshop and show leadership that the team has converged on a concrete set of requirements for the pilot; she is worried that if too many items are reframed as optional design choices, the project will look underdefined and lose executive confidence.
hidden_assumptions: Items repeatedly requested by sales, support, and compliance during discovery are legitimate 'requirements' for the pilot even if they are not externally mandated.
When people say the MVP should reflect the 'current onboarding process,' they mean the high-touch enterprise workflow currently handled through customer success spreadsheets and email approvals.
An 'audit trail' in onboarding includes something customer admins can see or export, because visibility reduced escalations in her operations experience.
A feature can be considered 'pilot-ready' if the product experience works for the two design partners and the internal team can manually cover rough edges during the pilot.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Backend platform engineering, service integration, release planning, internal tooling
members.background: Leo has led several infrastructure-heavy projects at CloudCore and is responsible for the services that provision customer tenants, connect identity systems, and emit compliance logs; he favors minimizing early commitments until technical constraints are proven.
members.private_state: Leo wants to avoid locking the team into accidental product commitments disguised as requirements and keep the pilot small enough to build safely in one sprint; he is concerned that broad interpretations of scope will create hidden dependencies on UI, ops, and compliance teams.
hidden_assumptions: A 'requirements' document should contain only constraints that are externally binding or technically necessary, while workflow and UX choices should remain flexible until validated.

The 'current onboarding process' refers to the more recent internal service desk flow documented by engineering for sandbox and tenant setup, since that is the only process he considers stable enough to mirror.
An 'audit trail' for the MVP means backend event logging with immutable timestamps sufficient for internal traceability and SOC2 evidence, not necessarily a customer-facing history view.
Something is 'pilot-ready' when it is deployed behind a feature flag, passes the normal engineering quality gates, and does not depend on special-case manual intervention beyond standard support.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about turning the workshop output into the 'requirements' for the MVP.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the consolidated set of stakeholder-requested fields, approval steps, visibility needs, and workflow expectations that the pilot should implement unless explicitly deferred.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means only the non-negotiable constraints such as SSO integration, tenant provisioning hooks, and compliance logging, with the rest treated as provisional design choices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are used to cross-functional teams saying 'requirements' as a neutral planning term, so the word feels shared and does not trigger clarification even though each person silently applies a different threshold for inclusion.

misalignment_points.topic: Which existing process the MVP should mirror
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the portal should follow the 'current onboarding process' so internal teams are not disrupted.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the enterprise customer onboarding sequence run by customer success, including account owner approval, security questionnaire upload, and provisioning status updates shared with the customer.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the engineering-documented internal service desk workflow used to create tenants and connect identity providers, which omits several customer-facing coordination steps.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume there is a single obvious current process because each spends time with a different operational slice of onboarding, and the phrase sounds concrete enough that neither thinks to name the specific artifact or team.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in audit trail
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the MVP needs an 'audit trail' for onboarding actions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the scope includes a visible history in the portal showing who submitted, approved, or changed onboarding data, plus timestamps that customer admins or support can review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the scope includes only backend event emission and storage for internal compliance review, with no portal history screen or export capability in the MVP.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Audit trail sounds like a standard compliance-oriented item, so each person hears the phrase as settled and fills in the implementation boundary from their own experience without restating it.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of pilot-ready by end of sprint
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on getting the portal 'pilot-ready by the end of the sprint' for two design partners.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means the design partners can complete onboarding through the portal with internal staff manually handling exceptions behind the scenes if needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means the feature is technically deployable under standard release conditions and can run without ad hoc operational workarounds beyond ordinary monitoring and support.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often use 'pilot-ready' as a reassuring milestone label rather than a formally defined acceptance state, so both interpret it through their usual release norms while hearing the other's agreement as confirmation.

turns.inner_thought: I need this meeting to end with a real scope, not another round of abstract principles. The workshop already gave us enough to call these requirements for the pilot: the fields, approvals, visibility expectations, and the audit trail stakeholders kept repeating. If I leave too much as 'to be designed later,' leadership will think we still haven't converged. And I want us confidently telling the design partners we're pilot-ready by the end of the sprint, even if support and CS have to smooth over some edges during the first runs.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. My goal today is pretty simple: lock the MVP requirements from last week's workshop, assign owners, and leave with a clear plan to get the onboarding portal pilot-ready by the end of the sprint for the two design partners.

turns.inner_thought: Fine as long as 'requirements' means the true must-haves: provisioning hooks, identity integration, compliance logging, and anything technically necessary to launch safely. I do not want a workshop wish list turning into accidental commitments. And 'pilot-ready' needs to mean something we can actually ship under a flag through normal QA, not a half-built flow propped up by side work from three teams.
turns.utterance: Yep, that makes sense. I think if we use this session to pull out the real requirements needed to support the pilot safely, we can keep the first cut lean and still hit that pilot-ready-by-end-of-sprint target.

turns.inner_thought: The biggest thing is not disrupting sales or customer success. The portal should mirror the enterprise onboarding sequence they already run manually: approvals, collecting security materials, and keeping the customer updated on status. If the design partners see a different rhythm, we'll create confusion immediately.
turns.utterance: Right, and from the go-to-market side, I want the portal to follow the current onboarding process so sales and customer success don't have to relearn anything for these first two accounts.

turns.inner_thought: That's reasonable. If we mirror the current onboarding process, we can anchor this in the engineering service desk flow that's already documented and stable: tenant creation, identity setup, and the provisioning sequence. Reusing that path reduces risk and keeps us from inventing a separate operational model for the pilot.
turns.utterance: Agreed. If we're following the current onboarding process, the cleanest path is to wire the portal into the same provisioning and identity setup steps we're already using so internal teams aren't dealing with a parallel flow.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep the stakeholder asks intact in the requirements doc. Approver visibility and an audit trail were not random nice-to-haves; they came up over and over from sales, support, and compliance because people lose track of who approved what and customers ask for status constantly. For the pilot, that visibility needs to be part of the portal experience, not just something hidden internally.
turns.utterance: One thing I don't want to lose from the workshop is that the requirements should keep approver visibility and an audit trail. Those were repeated enough times that I think they need to stay in scope, and they cut down on a lot of back-and-forth during onboarding.

turns.inner_thought: Audit trail is fine if we mean event logging in the backend. We already emit a lot of the needed signals, and extending that for onboarding actions is low risk. I still don't want to imply a bunch of UI or reporting work unless we prove we need it, but I don't hear Nina objecting to the lean interpretation, so we're aligned enough to proceed.
turns.utterance: I agree the MVP needs an audit trail. From engineering's side, we can emit the relevant events as part of the normal provisioning flow, so that piece shouldn't add much risk if we treat it as part of the core path.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds settled. I'll turn the workshop output into a proper requirements doc with acceptance notes so nobody reopens scope later. Once that's out, I can tell the design partners we expect the portal to be pilot-ready by the end of the sprint. Even if some rough spots need manual handling behind the scenes, they'll have a usable flow and we'll preserve momentum.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll finalize the requirements doc and the acceptance notes today so we can update the design partners that the pilot should be ready by the end of the sprint.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that timeline if we're disciplined about the bar. Pilot-ready needs to mean the feature is deployed behind a flag, through QA, and the main provisioning path is stable on the normal release process. I don't want a promise that depends on unusual manual operations or one-off interventions to keep it standing up.
turns.utterance: That timing works for me, as long as pilot-ready means the flagged deployment is through QA and the core provisioning path is stable on the existing release process.

turns.inner_thought: That's compatible with how I plan to message it. Support can absorb the exceptions while the design partners go through the current onboarding process in the portal; that's exactly what pilots are for. I don't need every operational edge removed before launch, just enough of the experience in place that the two customers can use it and we can learn from it.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll own the doc and the stakeholder follow-up, and I'll make sure support is lined up to cover any rough edges while the design partners go through the current onboarding process in the new portal.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take backend integration, provisioning hooks, identity wiring, and the logging work. As far as I'm concerned, we now have the essential requirements captured, and anything beyond that should stay flexible until we get pilot feedback. Better to prove the narrow version first than accidentally commit engineering to a wider product surface.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll take the backend integration and logging workstream. I think we have the essential requirements for the MVP, and we can keep the rest flexible until we learn from the pilot.
